breakfast.name: Hojaldras (Fried Bread)
instructions: Mix dough, rest
Flatten pieces
Deep fry until golden and puffy
breakfast.description: Puffy fried bread — Panamanian morning essential.

breakfast.name: Tortilla Panameña (Corn Cake)
instructions: Mix corn with salt and butter
Shape thick flat cakes
Fry until golden on both sides
breakfast.description: Thick fried corn cakes — not tortillas in the Mexican sense.

breakfast.name: Tortilla Panameña (Thick Corn Cake)
ingredients: Ground corn (pre-cooked corn flour — masarepa style)
instructions: The Panamanian tortilla is NOT the thin Mexican tortilla — it's a thick, fried corn cake
More like an arepa: thick, golden-crusted, soft inside
Shape the dough into thick rounds — about 1cm thick
Fry in oil or butter until golden on both sides — a crispy crust forms
The inside stays soft and corn-flavored — the outside is crunchy
Eaten for breakfast with cheese, eggs, or alongside soups
This thick corn cake is the base carb of Panamanian rural breakfast
The distinction from Mexican tortillas confuses visitors but is important — different food, same word
breakfast.description: Panama's thick corn cake (NOT a thin Mexican tortilla) — more like an arepa: ground corn formed into thick rounds, fried until golden-crusted outside and soft inside. The base carb of rural Panamanian breakfast, eaten with cheese or eggs. Same word, different food — the distinction matters.

breakfast.name: Carimañola (Yuca Fritter)
ingredients: Ground beef (seasoned with onion, garlic, cumin, tomato)
instructions: Carimañolas are Panama's yuca fritters — torpedo-shaped, meat-filled, fried golden
Boil yuca until very soft, mash until smooth — this becomes the outer shell
Season ground beef with onion, garlic, cumin, tomato — the filling
Shape the yuca dough around the meat filling — torpedo/football shape
Deep-fry until golden brown — the yuca crust becomes crispy
Inside: savory seasoned beef wrapped in smooth, starchy yuca
Carimañolas are breakfast food and street food — sold at fondas (street stalls)
The yuca must be perfectly mashed — lumps ruin the texture
Carimañolas are a gift from Afro-Panamanian cuisine — the Caribbean coast tradition
breakfast.description: Panama's torpedo-shaped fritter — boiled yuca mashed and shaped around seasoned ground beef, deep-fried until golden-crispy. Afro-Panamanian Caribbean coast tradition. The yuca must be perfectly smooth — lumps ruin the texture. Sold at fondas (street stalls) for breakfast. Crispy starchy outside, savory beef inside.

lunch.name: Sancocho Panameño (Chicken Stew)
instructions: Boil chicken with onion, garlic
Add root vegetables and corn
Simmer 30 min
Add lots of culantro
Serve with white rice
lunch.description: Panama's national dish — herby chicken soup with root vegetables.

lunch.name: Arroz con Pollo
instructions: Brown chicken with sofrito and achiote
Add rice and broth
Add vegetables and olives
Cook covered until done

lunch.name: Arroz con Pollo Panameño
ingredients: Sofrito: onion, garlic, bell pepper, tomato, culantro (recao)
instructions: Panamanian arroz con pollo uses achiote (annatto) for its distinctive orange-golden color
The sofrito base: onion, garlic, bell pepper, tomato, and culantro (recao — wide-leaf cilantro)
Culantro is NOT cilantro — it's a different plant with broader leaves and stronger flavor
Olives and capers are the Spanish colonial influence — they add brininess
Brown chicken, build sofrito, add rice and stock with achiote
The rice turns golden-orange from the achiote — the color is the identity
Arroz con pollo is the Panamanian Sunday lunch — families gather around the pot
Served with plátano maduro (fried sweet plantain) on the side — always
This is Latin American comfort food with Panama's specific flavoring: culantro + achiote
lunch.description: Panama's Sunday family rice — chicken with golden-orange rice (colored by achiote/annatto), flavored with culantro (recao — stronger than cilantro), olives, and capers (Spanish colonial legacy). Always served with plátano maduro (fried sweet plantain). The culantro + achiote combination is Panama's flavor identity. Families gather around this pot on Sundays.

lunch.name: Ropa Vieja Panameña (Shredded Beef Stew)
ingredients: Flank steak (boiled until tender, then shredded)
Worcestershire sauce (salsa inglesa — the Panamanian touch)
instructions: Ropa vieja means 'old clothes' — the shredded beef resembles tattered fabric
The beef is boiled for 1-2 hours until tender, then shredded along the grain
The shredded beef is sautéed with peppers, tomato, onion, garlic, and spices
Worcestershire sauce (salsa inglesa) is a distinctly Panamanian addition — Canal Zone influence
The American presence during the Canal construction brought Worcestershire sauce to Panama
Capers and olives: the Spanish layer in the dish
Ropa vieja is served over white rice with plátano maduro — the complete plate
This dish is shared across the Caribbean and Latin America — Cuban ropa vieja is the most famous
Panama's version is gentler, less tomato-heavy than Cuban, with the Worcestershire distinction
lunch.description: Panama's 'old clothes' — flank steak boiled tender, shredded, and sautéed with bell peppers, tomato, olives, capers, and Worcestershire sauce (salsa inglesa — a distinctly Panamanian addition from Canal Zone American influence). Served over rice with plátano maduro. Shared across the Caribbean; Panama's version is gentler, less tomato-heavy than Cuban, with the Worcestershire distinction.

lunch.name: Ceviche Panameño
ingredients: Corvina (sea bass — very fresh, diced small)
instructions: Panamanian ceviche is distinct from Peruvian — different proportions, different style
The fish (corvina is the classic) is marinated LONGER than Peruvian ceviche — 30+ minutes
This longer cure makes the fish more opaque — a different texture than Peruvian raw-style
The Panamanian addition: CELERY — diced celery adds crunch and freshness
Ají chombo (Scotch bonnet pepper) provides the heat — Caribbean-style hot
Panamanian ceviche is street food — sold in small plastic cups on the street
The Casco Viejo (Old Town) in Panama City is ceviche territory — vendors everywhere
Served with saltine crackers (galletas de soda) — not tostones, not chips
Panama's position (connecting Central and South America) gives its ceviche a unique identity
lunch.description: Panama's street ceviche — corvina (sea bass) diced small, cured in lime juice longer than Peruvian style (more opaque texture), with the distinctly Panamanian addition of diced celery for crunch, red onion, cilantro, and ají chombo (Scotch bonnet heat). Served in small plastic cups with saltine crackers. Casco Viejo vendors everywhere. Panama's geographic bridge position gives its ceviche a unique identity.

dinner.name: Corvina al Ajillo (Garlic Sea Bass)
instructions: Sauté lots of garlic in butter
Add fish, cook 3 min per side
Deglaze with wine
Garnish with parsley
dinner.description: Pan-seared sea bass in garlic butter.

dinner.name: Tamales Panameños
instructions: Make seasoned masa
Fill with chicken, olives, capers, raisins
Wrap in bijao leaves
Boil 90 min
dinner.description: Large tamales wrapped in bijao leaves.

dinner.name: Tamales Panameños
ingredients: Filling: chicken or pork, onion, bell pepper, tomato, olives, capers, raisins
Bijao leaves (or banana leaves — for wrapping)
instructions: Panamanian tamales are wrapped in bijao leaves — a specific tropical plant leaf
The bijao leaf gives a distinctive flavor different from banana leaf or corn husk
The masa is enriched with achiote — giving it an orange-golden color
The filling: chicken or pork with the Panamanian flavor profile (olives, capers, raisins)
The raisin is the sweet surprise inside — the sweet-savory balance
Shape the masa on the leaf, add filling, fold and tie with string
Steam for 2 hours — the tamale sets inside the leaf
Tamales in Panama are Christmas food — made in December, communally, in large batches
The tamalada: the family gathers to make 50-100+ tamales for Christmas
Everyone has a role: masa maker, filler, wrapper, tier — communal production
Panamanian tamales are large — substantial, a meal in themselves
The bijao leaf wrapping is environmentally specific — bijao grows in Panama's tropical forests
dinner.description: Panama's Christmas tamale — golden-orange masa (colored with achiote) filled with chicken or pork, olives, capers, and raisins (the sweet surprise), wrapped in bijao leaves (a specific tropical leaf with a distinctive flavor), steamed 2 hours. Made communally in December: the tamalada, 50-100+ tamales, everyone with a role. Large, substantial — a meal in themselves.

dinner.name: Guacho (Soupy Rice Stew)
ingredients: Tomato, onion, garlic, bell pepper, culantro
instructions: Guacho is Panama's soupy rice — wetter than arroz con pollo, thicker than soup
The name may come from 'guachada' — a mix, a stew-soup hybrid
The rice cooks IN the stew — absorbing all the flavor, releasing starch
The starch makes the liquid slightly thick — not a clear soup, not a dry rice
On the Caribbean coast (Bocas del Toro, Colón), guacho includes coconut milk
The coconut milk version is Afro-Panamanian — the Caribbean culinary identity
Guacho can be seafood (shrimp, octopus), chicken, or sausage — flexible
Culantro (recao) is the essential herb — more pungent than cilantro
Guacho is comfort food — a one-pot meal that feeds a crowd
It represents Panama's cultural synthesis: Indigenous, Spanish, African, Caribbean
dinner.description: Panama's soupy rice stew — rice cooked in a tomato-culantro broth with seafood, chicken, or sausage, releasing starch until neither soup nor dry rice. The Caribbean coast version (Bocas del Toro, Colón) adds coconut milk — Afro-Panamanian culinary identity. One-pot comfort that feeds a crowd. Panama's cultural synthesis: Indigenous, Spanish, African, Caribbean in one dish.

dinner.name: Patacones con Todo (Tostones)
ingredients: Toppings: shredded beef, ceviche, cheese, hogao (tomato-onion sauce)
instructions: Patacones are twice-fried green plantain discs — tostones — Panama's essential side and snack
Slice green plantain into thick rounds — fry once until soft (not golden)
Remove, smash flat with a tostonera (plantain press) or the bottom of a glass
Fry AGAIN until golden and crispy — the double-frying is essential
The result: crispy, starchy, slightly salty discs
In Panama, patacones are 'con todo' — topped with everything
Shredded beef (carne desmechada), ceviche, cheese, hogao (tomato-onion sauce)
Patacones replace bread, replace chips, replace tortillas — they ARE the vessel
Every Panamanian meal can include patacones — the universal accompaniment
The tostonera (press) is in every Panamanian kitchen — a dedicated single-purpose tool
dinner.description: Panama's universal vessel — green plantain sliced, fried once, SMASHED flat with a tostonera, fried AGAIN until golden-crispy. Topped with everything: shredded beef, ceviche, cheese, hogao (tomato-onion sauce). Patacones replace bread, chips, and tortillas. Every Panamanian kitchen has a tostonera. The double-frying technique makes them crispy-starchy and addictive.

snacks.name: Carimañolas
instructions: Mash yuca, shape around meat filling
Seal into oval shapes
Deep fry until golden
snacks.description: Yuca fritters stuffed with seasoned beef.

snacks.name: Empanadas Panameñas
ingredients: Filling: ground beef, onion, bell pepper, garlic, cumin, tomato
instructions: Panamanian empanadas use corn dough — not wheat flour dough
The corn dough gives a grainier, slightly sweet, distinctive texture
The filling: ground beef seasoned with onion, pepper, garlic, cumin, tomato
Shape into half-moons — press edges to seal with a fork
Deep-fry until golden — the corn crust puffs slightly
Panamanian empanadas are smaller than Argentine — snack-sized, eaten on the go
Sold at fondas, markets, bus stops — the everywhere street food
The corn empanada tradition connects to pre-colonial Mesoamerican corn culture
Simple, cheap, satisfying — the after-school snack, the bus-ride food
snacks.description: Panama's corn-dough empanada — ground beef in corn masa (grainier, sweeter than wheat flour dough), fried golden until the crust puffs slightly. Smaller and snack-sized — eaten on the go. Sold at fondas, markets, and bus stops. The corn empanada tradition connects to pre-colonial Mesoamerican culture. Simple, cheap, the after-school snack.

snacks.name: Hojaldras (Fried Bread)
instructions: Hojaldras are Panama's fried bread — puffy, golden, slightly sweet
The dough: enriched with butter, milk, egg — rolled and cut into rounds or rectangles
Deep-fried until puffed and golden — the dough balloons from the heat
The result: light, airy, slightly sweet fried bread
Hojaldras are breakfast food — eaten with cheese, eggs, or dipped in coffee
They're also sold at fondas alongside empanadas and carimañolas
The puffiness is the mark of well-made hojaldras — flat ones are wrong
Hojaldras represent the Spanish fried-dough tradition adapted in Panama
Every Panamanian child remembers hojaldras at grandma's breakfast table
snacks.description: Panama's puffy fried bread — enriched dough (butter, milk, egg) deep-fried until it balloons golden and airy. Slightly sweet. Eaten for breakfast with cheese or eggs, or dipped in coffee. Sold at fondas alongside empanadas. The puffiness is the quality mark — flat ones are wrong. Every Panamanian child's grandma-breakfast memory.

snacks.name: Raspao (Shaved Ice)
ingredients: Fruit syrups: tamarind, passion fruit, guanábana, cherry
instructions: Raspao is Panama's shaved ice — the street drink that survives the tropical heat
Vendors push carts through neighborhoods — the sound of ice being shaved signals them
Finely shave a block of ice — snow-fine texture
Drizzle with fruit syrups — the choice of syrup is personal
Top with condensed milk — the sweetness is deliberate
Raspao vendors are a fixture of Panamanian street life — they appear in the heat of the day
The tamarind syrup version is the most traditionally Panamanian
Raspao is democratic — costs almost nothing, accessible to everyone
The neon-colored syrup dripping down the cup is visually striking
snacks.description: Panama's heat survival — finely shaved ice drenched in fruit syrups (tamarind is most traditional; also passion fruit, guanábana) and drizzled with condensed milk. Vendors push carts through neighborhoods — the sound of ice being shaved signals them. Costs almost nothing. Democratic refreshment in Panama's tropical heat. The neon-colored syrup dripping down the cup is visually striking.

desserts.name: Tres Leches Cake
instructions: Bake sponge cake
Poke holes, pour three-milk mixture over
Refrigerate overnight
Top with whipped cream and cinnamon

desserts.name: Tres Leches Cake (Panamanian Style)
ingredients: Sponge cake: flour, eggs, sugar, vanilla
Three milks: evaporated milk, condensed milk, heavy cream
instructions: Tres leches (three milks cake) is beloved across Latin America — Panama claims a version
The sponge cake is baked plain, then SOAKED in a mixture of three milks
The three milks: evaporated milk + condensed milk + heavy cream — poured over the warm cake
The cake absorbs the milks — becoming incredibly moist, almost pudding-like
A properly soaked tres leches should be wet but still hold its shape
Top with whipped cream — the lightness contrasts with the dense, milky cake
Panamanian tres leches is often served at birthdays and celebrations
The cake must rest overnight — the soaking time allows full absorption
Tres leches is the Latin American dessert that surprises outsiders: wet cake is intentional
The cinnamon dusting on top is the final touch
desserts.description: Panama's celebration cake — sponge cake soaked in three milks (evaporated, condensed, heavy cream) until impossibly moist, topped with whipped cream and cinnamon. The wetness is intentional — a properly soaked tres leches is almost pudding-like. Must rest overnight for full absorption. Beloved across Latin America; Panama serves it at birthdays and celebrations.

desserts.name: Dulce de Coco (Coconut Sweet)
instructions: Dulce de coco is Panama's simple coconut candy — grated coconut cooked in sugar syrup
Grate fresh coconut — the freshness matters enormously
Cook grated coconut with sugar, water, cinnamon, and vanilla
Stir continuously as the sugar caramelizes and the coconut absorbs it
The mixture thickens into a sticky, caramelized coconut mass
Shape into small balls or patties — they set as they cool
The flavor: intense coconut, caramel, cinnamon — deeply sweet
Dulce de coco is sold at markets, fairs, and by home cooks
The simple ingredients belie the skill: knowing when to stop cooking is the art
Afro-Panamanian coconut traditions from the Caribbean coast influence this dessert
desserts.description: Panama's coconut candy — freshly grated coconut cooked with sugar, cinnamon, and vanilla until the sugar caramelizes and the coconut absorbs it into a sticky, intense confection. Shaped into balls or patties. The art: knowing when to stop cooking. Afro-Panamanian Caribbean coast tradition. Sold at markets and fairs. Simple ingredients, skilled execution.

drinks.name: Chicha de Maracuyá (Passion Fruit Drink)
instructions: Blend passion fruit pulp with water and sugar
Strain
Serve over ice

drinks.name: Seco Herrerano
instructions: Pour seco over ice
Add milk, stir
drinks.description: Panama's national spirit mixed with milk — yes, really.

drinks.name: Chicha de Piña (Pineapple Drink)
ingredients: Pineapple (rind and flesh — the rind has more flavor)
instructions: Chicha de piña is Panama's pineapple drink — the most popular chicha
The pineapple RIND is used — it has more concentrated flavor than the flesh
Boil pineapple rind (and some flesh) with sugar and optional spices
Let cool, strain, serve over ice — the drink is golden and intensely tropical
Chicha de piña is at every fonda, restaurant, and home table
The fermented version exists too — left to ferment, it becomes mildly alcoholic
But the non-alcoholic fresh version is the everyday drink
Chicha (fermented corn drink) is pre-colonial — chicha de piña adapted the concept
The pineapple rind waste reduction is practical and flavorful — zero-waste cooking
drinks.description: Panama's everyday refreshment — pineapple drink made from boiled pineapple RIND (more concentrated flavor than flesh), sugar, and optional cinnamon. Golden, intensely tropical, served ice-cold. At every fonda, restaurant, and home table. The fermented version becomes mildly alcoholic. Zero-waste cooking: the rind that would be discarded becomes the best part.
